{"answer": "# Feasibility assessment: two mobile cobots for LPBF and CNC tending

**Bottom line.** The proposed UR12e-class arm on a MiR250 can plausibly perform *engineered, repeatable exchanges* of the small printer’s plates, cartridges, drawers, jars and 2.5 kg module. It should not be expected to operate an as-built machine with human-style latches, exposed 200 °C parts, loose powder and tight unregistered fits. Two such robots could automate selected assembly steps and repetitive Haas VF-series loading, but the evidence does **not** support a claim that they could autonomously build the whole printer or execute an arbitrary prototype machining job. These are engineering judgments, not measured success rates for the proposed cell. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000065)

## 1. What LPBF automation has actually demonstrated

| Example | What worked—and what it does not establish |
|---|---|
| **HyProCell: ADIRA LPBF, EROWA robot and Haas VF-2.** Its LPBF machine gained a robot-access door, seals and automated in-chamber vacuuming. An EROWA ERD 500 transferred pallets among the printer, SOLUKON powder-removal station, magazine and Haas VF-2; a dust box contained powder during transfers. Substrate plates were **screwed to a common handling pallet**, rather than being grasped by their printed edges. The smallest CNC chamber constrained pallet size to **400 × 500 mm**. A dedicated telescopic handler accommodated loads up to **300 kg**; the reported **2 µm** is precision *after its dedicated clamp engages*, not free-space robot accuracy. A roughly **20 m** integrated layout was impractical, so scanning remained outside the physical cell. This is the closest published printer-to-Haas analogue, but uses substantial fixed industrial handling equipment, not a mobile cobot. | (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000077) |
| **Additive Industries MetalFAB1.** An Exchange Module and robot handle build plates and products; optional modules support job change, materials and post-processing. The described three-module printer has a **420 × 420 × 400 mm** build envelope. The account does not specify the gripper, latch geometry or a measured exchange success rate. | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000017) |
| **LPBF-to-CNC zero-point interface.** Boivie and colleagues put EROWA chucks in an LPBF machine and CNC mill. Their PowerChuck P uses a **10,000 N spring clamp**, pneumatic release and **0.002 mm manufacturer-specified** pallet repeatability. Milling trials found adequate stability, but coolant migrated beneath the pallet: the interface had to be cleaned before returning to LPBF. This is precisely why the *machine fixture*, not the robot, must establish the printing and machining datums. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022) |
| **Alternative part interfaces.** Ferchow and colleagues validated LPBF-integrated sacrificial bolts that act as gripping/machining datums: **250 N** produced at most **12.5 µm** displacement in one test. Their separate sheet-metal carrier reduced re-clamped deformation but measured part-position deviations up to **0.23 mm**. Even excellent fixture repeatability does not remove printed-part deformation or recoater-clearance concerns. | (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023) |

**Powder work is a separate automation problem.** Commercial examples combine closed powder circulation, vacuum transfer, machine-side unpacking and programmed depowdering—not an ordinary gripper carrying an open jar. ADIRA’s described system used four vacuum conveying systems; HyProCell combined in-machine vacuuming with part-specific SOLUKON programs. Automated sieving and recirculation exist, but recovery must track alloy, batch, reuse, contamination and environmental exposure. A studied semi-automatic unpacker found that internal cavities and intervening part walls obstruct vacuum removal; adding vacuum points showed diminishing benefit beyond four in its simulated arrangement. Fine metal powders present exposure, contamination and, for applicable alloys, fire/explosion hazards. Qualify sealed reservoirs, contained overflow disposal and powder-specific cleaning with the actual alloy safety data; do not infer that a standard wrist camera, vacuum cup or cobot is suitable inside a contaminated chamber. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015)

## 2. Docking, registration and achievable insertion

**Do not equate navigation, docking, arm repeatability and finished placement.** In a *MiR250-based* laboratory manipulator, reported base odometry precision was approximately **±50 mm**; typical vision/SLAM positioning was described as approximately **±10 mm**. The researchers consequently navigated to a station, localized a station marker, imaged an instrument marker with a wrist camera and touched instrument reference faces to register its frame. Their resulting plate handover precision was **±1.2 mm**; this is a *whole-system instrument-relative result*, not a MiR250 docking-repeatability specification or a result for the proposed UR12e. An independent **non-MiR** fiducial-docking study reported, over **1,500** trials, position-distribution ranges of **8.4 mm in x and 4.7 mm in y**, versus **61.9 and 8.5 mm** for navigation alone; these are ranges, not guaranteed absolute errors. A NIST mobile-manipulator calibration study still reported approximately **1.19 mm mean-square residual** and demonstrated that end-effectors could get within a few millimetres of targets after base-to-arm registration. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000043)

**Design target, explicitly an estimate:** make the MiR park repeatably enough to see a *machine-mounted* datum; calibrate camera-to-tool and arm-to-base transforms; re-observe that datum **after every arrival and after every vertical-lift move**; and use guarded, force-limited final insertion into lead-ins. Budget approximately **1–3 mm instrument-relative approach error as an initial development target**, to be measured across stations, lift heights, temperatures and loaded arms—not as a manufacturer guarantee. Reserve **submillimetre final seating** for passive datums/zero-point clamps plus verified closure, not visual open-loop positioning. As evidence that insertion tolerance can exceed free-space pose accuracy, a UR5 study inserted a **15.97 mm** unchamfered peg into a **16.07 mm** unchamfered hole using a specialized compliant search; success depended on initial offset and tilt, and one **5 mm** offset case failed where **2 mm** succeeded. It is not evidence that this MiR/UR/gripper combination can routinely insert a 0.1 mm-clearance pin. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000052)

## 3. Design the printer and tools around the robot

The stated **12.5 kg arm payload and 1,300 mm reach** are useful screening inputs, but the **Robotiq 2F-85 is separately rated for 5 kg**: published specifications give **85 mm stroke**, **20–235 N programmable grip force** and about **0.9 kg gripper mass**. Include camera, changer, fingers, wiring, carried part, centre-of-gravity offset and acceleration in the *robot* payload calculation; do not interpret 235 N jaw force as a 235 N capacity for pulling a stuck door. A design study found that tool mass and a **260 mm** flange offset reduced usable payload substantially, illustrating why reach and wrist moment must be checked in each posture. For the **2.5 kg** module, nominal mass alone passes the gripper’s 5 kg rating, but an open powder container, awkward grasp, dynamic moment or hot/smooth surface can still make the grasp unsuitable. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049)

Provide a positively retained **cool-side metal handling tab or insulated carrier** for each plate; put printed parts and the plate in a tray or sealed transport cassette. A plate directly at **200 °C** requires a qualified thermal barrier, gripper-finger material and dwell-time test: neither the cited 2F-85 data nor the vacuum-gripper study establishes 200 °C operation. If using suction on *cool, clean* flat panels, provide a dedicated vacuum circuit, nonporous land, pressure confirmation and a mechanical drop catch; powder, rough surfaces and heat make suction alone a poor default. Use a changer with positively sensed tool-lock and available electrical/pneumatic pass-throughs for separate jaw, broad-plate, module-hook and cleaning tools. These are proposed design controls, not documented capabilities of the specified off-the-shelf gripper. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000072)

For the **drop-down O-ring door**, put its operating handle outside the door’s swept arc; support its weight with a hinge counterbalance/gas strut or powered actuator, and use mechanically indexed latches or pneumatic compression rather than asking the wrist to develop seal preload. Provide door-open/closed and seal/latch sensors, and prevent the door from obstructing the floor-module extraction path. For **25–75 mm plates**, standardize the *carrier* datum and robot pickup location even if plate diameters change: use an indexed bayonet driven by a dedicated keyed tool only if its seating torque and powder tolerance are tested; a pneumatically released drawbar or zero-point chuck moves the high preload into the fixture. Design each **reservoir, recoater cartridge, cover-slide drawer, overflow jar and removable liner** with a generous grasp tab, a prescribed single extraction direction, captive detents, tapered entry/lead-ins and observable seated/unseated states. Add locating cones/kinematic features where repeatability matters, keep powder off reference lands, and support drawers and liners so extraction does not bind. These are application-specific recommendations derived from demonstrated benefits of common pallets, positive fixture datums, compliant insertion and contamination control—not published validation of the proposed printer. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052)

**Force budget:** a published specification for the *UR10e* gives force-mode control up to **100 N**, nominal **5.5 N** force accuracy. In actual surface-finishing experiments, **100 N** was commanded, but mean absolute tracking errors were about **10.6–12.5 N** in direct-contact tests; rapidly changing contact could briefly lose contact or overshoot. Treat **100 N as documented UR10e force-mode capability, not a guaranteed UR12e force at every posture, door-opening rating, safe human-contact limit or justification to pry a jammed mechanism**. Set substantially lower task-specific search limits and verify them experimentally. A pneumatic robotic CNC vise illustrates the alternative: at **6 bar**, its lever-assisted actuator produced about **5.1 kN** clamping force with **0.35 s** clamp time, while the robot only loaded the part. A sprung latch, counterbalanced door, powered clamp and instrumented release similarly separate manipulation force from process force. Safety contact limits require their own risk assessment: constrained pinch contacts are particularly hazardous even with a cobot. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000068)

## 4. Haas tending and two-robot assembly

**Realistic CNC scope:** automate loading a known blank or standardized pallet, actuating an *interlocked* powered door and pneumatic vise, checking part and clamp presence, calling an already proved CNC program, unloading a part, and performing a defined cleaning/probing sequence. A robotic vise demonstrator used CNC-door/robot/clamp interlocks and reported approximately **±0.01 mm** repeatability of its fixture resets; a Haas-containing LPBF hybrid cell used a VF-2 and dedicated EROWA pallet transfer. Neither demonstrates that a MiR-mounted UR12e with a 2F-85 can operate an unmodified Haas door or hand-tighten a milling vise. A separate Haas-cell example moved **6–8 kg** castings with a **10 kg** KUKA robot and purpose-designed pneumatic three-jaw tool: these loads exceed the cited 2F-85’s **5 kg** rating. (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000076, pqac-00000077)

**Expect chips, coolant and setup to dominate reliability.** In one CNC robotic-loading implementation, chips caused imperfect part seating, washing-emulsion viscosity changed cleaning effectiveness, and slight vise-height differences upset alignment. Wrong part placement and incorrect robot recipes caused collisions and manual resets; its approximately **12-minute** unload/clean/load cycle was reported, while **140 operating hours per week was an objective, not an immediately achieved result**. For a *prototype* printer, engineers must still generate and prove CAM, set tooling and work offsets, design fixture jaws for changing parts, inspect first articles and correct unexpected burrs or chips. **Estimated scope—not a published percentage:** a deliberately palletized, repetitive family might automate *most repeated load/unload cycles*, but an arbitrary one-off prototype may have only **roughly 10–30% of its distinct setup/assembly operations** readily robotizable without further fixtures and engineering. Do not present that illustrative planning range as observed throughput, machine utilization or fraction of machining time. (pqac-00000065, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000078)

For building the printer itself, two mobile arms may stage machined panels, hold a bracket while a second robot drives an accessible fastener, place standardized modules and perform prescribed functional checks. Neither a two-robot label nor simultaneous reach solves fine cable routing, optical/laser alignment, sealed gas connections, O-ring inspection, torque verification, precision recoater calibration or process qualification. Sequence a **single arm first** on one printer fixture and one CNC fixture; use the second only where the task demonstrably needs a supporting hand or parallel servicing. Two robots introduce shared-space collision, coordination and recovery problems. A published dual-UR10e system explicitly coordinated their shared workspace with joint planning, scene updates and replanning; its application was battery disassembly, not proof of fully automatic printer assembly. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000061)

## 5. Collision planning and safety practice

Create dimensioned CAD/URDF collision geometry for **both complete mobile manipulators**, including actual tools, camera, cable dress and each grasped plate/module as an attached object. In MoveIt’s planning scene, represent the printer enclosure, vertical-lift tray at *each commanded elevation*, door and drawer at *each commanded state*, Haas enclosure, fixture and tool rack. Check robot self-collision, robot–robot collision and all intermediate poses; check or conservatively approximate **swept volumes** of the door, drawer, trays, carried parts and arms, since checking only pickup and drop-off poses misses intervening collisions. Restrict arm movements to a verified parked-base pose and block navigation while an arm or machine aperture protrudes into a travel corridor. MoveIt/FCL has been demonstrated for two UR10e arms, with updated environmental depth data represented at **30 mm voxel** resolution; that is useful for broad obstacle avoidance but far too coarse to validate a plate edge or tight latch. A published UR/2F-85 MoveIt setup likewise explicitly models the gripper and worktable; custom dimensions and dynamic aperture states must be added for this cell. (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000079)

**Planning is not safeguarding.** Apply a cell-level risk assessment and independent machine/safety-controller interlocks for laser enable, inert-gas/powder conditions, temperature, printer and CNC doors, spindle stopped, fixture clamped, robot/base stationary, vertical-lift position and human access. Use appropriate guarding or safety-rated zones/stops around hot surfaces, falling modules, door pinch points, moving cutters and combustible or inhalable powder; a cobot’s power-and-force-limiting mode does not make these process hazards collaborative. Test failure and recovery states—including loss of power/air, dropped plate, incomplete clamp, open powder jar and an obstructed door—before unattended runs. ## 3. bonifazio2024automatedcncloadingunloading pages 13-18 (Context ID: pqac-00000078)

s meticulous data entry ensures that the robot can execute each phase of

the cycle with precision. The absence of artificial vision during raw part pick-

up is compensated by the strategic use of templates in the Modula drawer and

by leveraging the memory contained in the recipe, enabling the robot to

identify each part’s exact location quickly and accurately.


3.4.  Operational Phases

The work cycle of the robot is divided into three main phases: unloading,

cleaning, and loading. In the unloading phase, the robot removes the semi-

finished products first. To do this, it uses a tipper to rotate and position the

pieces on the inclined plane, ensuring that the unfinished surfaces are exposed

for easy gripping later. It then proceeds to unload the finished pieces, placing

them in another site of the inclined plane.

Once the unloading phase is complete, the system enters the cleaning phase.

The shutters of the bay close to allow a high-pressure emulsion jet from the

washing tank to remove any residual chips or debris from the pallet. This step

is essential to maintain quality and prevent damage during later stages of

machining.

During the loading phase, the robot first loads the semi-finished products back

onto the pallet, followed by the raw parts retrieved from the Modula vertical

warehouse. These raw parts are arranged in dedicated templates that ensure

precise positioning and repeatability during the robot’s gripping actions. The

use of these templates, combined with the detailed recipe data, eliminates

potential sources of error and significantly speeds up the entire cycle. The

robot then deposits the finished pieces in the Modula drawer, ready for further

handling or the next stages of production. Finally, the fully loaded pallet is

returned to the CNC machine, closing the cycle and ensuring continuous,




                                                                   11reliable productivity. The average cycle time for the robot to complete these

operations is approximately 12 minutes.


3.5.  The objective of reaching 140 weekly hours

The primary goal of introducing these robotic systems was to achieve 140

hours of weekly operational work per CNC machine, thereby ensuring

competitive pricing in the market. However, this target was not reached

immediately due to the challenges and inefficiencies encountered in the initial

implementation phase,  as  detailed  in the subsequent  chapters  of  this

dissertation. Addressing these issues through targeted improvements and

continuous  optimization  is key  to  reaching  this  140-hour  target and

maintaining Eurofluid hydraulic’s position as a competitive player in an

increasingly demanding market.


3.6.  Troubleshooting and System Improvements

Throughout my internship,  I worked closely with the technical team to

analyze inefficiencies and find solutions to enhance the system’s performance.

For instance, I addressed problems caused by slight variations in the base

heights of the vises, which could compromise the alignment of the pieces.

Residual chips in the pallet posed another challenge, occasionally affecting the

correct positioning of the semi-finished parts. Additionally, fluctuations in the

viscosity of the emulsion used for cleaning sometimes led to incomplete

cleaning cycles.

To address these challenges, we implemented new verification procedures,

such as an additional piece presence check in the Modula’s drawer using the

proximity  sensors on  the  robot’s  gripper.  This allowed  the  robot  to

automatically skip empty positions if a piece was missing or incorrectly placed



                                                                   12by the operator, ensuring that the loading phase could proceed without

disruptions and that the CNC machine received a complete pallet ready for

processing.

Safety has also been a primary consideration in this project. In addition to

collision detection systems on the robot, a manually operated emergency stop

button has been incorporated to allow operators to intervene and stop the

system immediately if anomalies occur.


3.7.  System Overview and Visual Representation

The schematic diagram of the robotic cell is shown in (Figure 6) This diagram

helps to understand the interaction between the different components.





Figure 6 . Schematic diagram of the robotic cell and control logic.

As explained in Figure 1, the interaction between the robot, the bays, and the

Modula vertical warehouse is managed by a Siemens PLC. The control logic

ensures precise communication and coordination.



                                                                   133.8.  Achieved objectives

Thanks to the training provided to the staff working in the company, we were

able to reduce, and in some cases almost eliminate, the situations in which the

robot stopped due to collision errors during the gripping of the raw parts, an

issue that previously caused frequent interruptions to the production process.

At the same time, the revision and improvement of the bay washing cycle

enabled the removal of any residual chips, eliminating the risk that these chips

could create unwanted thicknesses leading to out-of-tolerance parts and

subsequent blocks. Overall, these and the other solutions discussed in the

following chapters have drastically reduced unjustified interruptions in the

robot’s work  cycle, improved process continuity, and minimized piece

positioning errors. As a result, the production process has become more stable

and capable of progressively reaching the target of 140 working hours per

week for each CNC machine.

4.1.  Description of the production cycle

Eurofluid Hydraulic specializes in the production of customized hydraulic

blocks for clients operating in various industrial sectors. Upon receiving a

customer request, the production process follows one of two paths.  If a

detailed technical drawing  is provided, the programming office directly

processes it, generating and simulating the CNC code required for production.

In the absence of a drawing, the programming office develops a project based

on the customer’s specifications, producing both the technical drawing and

the CNC code.

Once the CNC program is ready, the proposal is sent to the production

planning office. Here, the team decides which machine will be assigned to the

job, based on the specific characteristics of the available equipment (Mori,

Mazak, Toyoda, and Kitamura), on the material, dimensions, and complexity

of the workpiece. The workload of each machine is also considered, to ensure

an even distribution of the weekly working hours.

The finalized production order ("launch") is then sent to the workshop, where

the tool's room and assembles the necessary tools. Following this, a first

sample is produced and sent to quality control. Only after approval, along

with any required adjustments, does full-scale production begin.

My  internship began  with  a  training  phase  designed  to  provide  a

comprehensive overview of the company’s operations. During the initial

weeks, I was move through the various departments, allowing me to observe

the workflow and understand the contribution of each sector to the overall

production process, from the receipt of customer specifications to the final

manufacturing stages.

After this general overview, I was supported by my company tutor, who

introduced me to the robotic arms used for loading and unloading parts in

       to avoid errors or collisions during operation.

{"answer": "# Feasibility assessment: two mobile cobots for LPBF and CNC tending

**Bottom line.** The proposed UR12e-class arm on a MiR250 can plausibly perform *engineered, repeatable exchanges* of the small printer’s plates, cartridges, drawers, jars and 2.5 kg module. Two such robots could automate selected assembly steps and repetitive Haas VF-series loading, but the evidence does **not** support a claim that they could autonomously build the whole printer or execute an arbitrary prototype machining job. These are engineering judgments, not measured success rates for the proposed cell. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000065)

## 1. What LPBF automation has actually demonstrated

| Example | What worked—and what it does not establish |
|---|---|
| **HyProCell: ADIRA LPBF, EROWA robot and Haas VF-2.** Its LPBF machine gained a robot-access door, seals and automated in-chamber vacuuming. An EROWA ERD 500 transferred pallets among the printer, SOLUKON powder-removal station, magazine and Haas VF-2; a dust box contained powder during transfers. Substrate plates were **screwed to a common handling pallet**, rather than being grasped by their printed edges. The smallest CNC chamber constrained pallet size to **400 × 500 mm**. A dedicated telescopic handler accommodated loads up to **300 kg**; the reported **2 µm** is precision *after its dedicated clamp engages*, not free-space robot accuracy. A roughly **20 m** integrated layout was impractical, so scanning remained outside the physical cell. This is the closest published printer-to-Haas analogue, but uses substantial fixed industrial handling equipment, not a mobile cobot. | (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000077) |
| **Additive Industries MetalFAB1.** An Exchange Module and robot handle build plates and products; optional modules support job change, materials and post-processing. The described three-module printer has a **420 × 420 × 400 mm** build envelope. The account does not specify the gripper, latch geometry or a measured exchange success rate. | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000017) |
| **LPBF-to-CNC zero-point interface.** Boivie and colleagues put EROWA chucks in an LPBF machine and CNC mill. Their PowerChuck P uses a **10,000 N spring clamp**, pneumatic release and **0.002 mm manufacturer-specified** pallet repeatability. Milling trials found adequate stability, but coolant migrated beneath the pallet: the interface had to be cleaned before returning to LPBF. This is precisely why the *machine fixture*, not the robot, must establish the printing and machining datums. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022) |
| **Alternative part interfaces.** Ferchow and colleagues validated LPBF-integrated sacrificial bolts that act as gripping/machining datums: **250 N** produced at most **12.5 µm** displacement in one test. Their separate sheet-metal carrier reduced re-clamped deformation but measured part-position deviations up to **0.23 mm**. Even excellent fixture repeatability does not remove printed-part deformation or recoater-clearance concerns. | (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021, pqac-00000023) |

**Powder work is a separate automation problem.** Commercial examples combine closed powder circulation, vacuum transfer, machine-side unpacking and programmed depowdering—not an ordinary gripper carrying an open jar. ADIRA’s described system used four vacuum conveying systems; HyProCell combined in-machine vacuuming with part-specific SOLUKON programs. Automated sieving and recirculation exist, but recovery must track alloy, batch, reuse, contamination and environmental exposure. A studied semi-automatic unpacker found that internal cavities and intervening part walls obstruct vacuum removal; adding vacuum points showed diminishing benefit beyond four in its simulated arrangement. Fine metal powders present exposure, contamination and, for applicable alloys, fire/explosion hazards. Qualify sealed reservoirs, contained overflow disposal and powder-specific cleaning with the actual alloy safety data; do not infer that a standard wrist camera, vacuum cup or cobot is suitable inside a contaminated chamber. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000011, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015)

## 2. Docking, registration and achievable insertion

**Do not equate navigation, docking, arm repeatability and finished placement.** In a *MiR250-based* laboratory manipulator, reported base odometry precision was approximately **±50 mm**; typical vision/SLAM positioning was described as approximately **±10 mm**. The researchers consequently navigated to a station, localized a station marker, imaged an instrument marker with a wrist camera and touched instrument reference faces to register its frame. Their resulting plate handover precision was **±1.2 mm**; this is a *whole-system instrument-relative result*, not a MiR250 docking-repeatability specification or a result for the proposed UR12e. An independent **non-MiR** fiducial-docking study reported, over **1,500** trials, position-distribution ranges of **8.4 mm in x and 4.7 mm in y**, versus **61.9 and 8.5 mm** for navigation alone; these are ranges, not guaranteed absolute errors. A NIST mobile-manipulator calibration study still reported approximately **1.19 mm mean-square residual** and demonstrated that end-effectors could get within a few millimetres of targets after base-to-arm registration. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000043)

**Design target, explicitly an estimate:** make the MiR park repeatably enough to see a *machine-mounted* datum; calibrate camera-to-tool and arm-to-base transforms; re-observe that datum **after every arrival and after every vertical-lift move**; and use guarded, force-limited final insertion into lead-ins. Budget approximately **1–3 mm instrument-relative approach error as an initial development target**, to be measured across stations, lift heights, temperatures and loaded arms—not as a manufacturer guarantee. Reserve **submillimetre final seating** for passive datums/zero-point clamps plus verified closure, not visual open-loop positioning. As evidence that insertion tolerance can exceed free-space pose accuracy, a UR5 study inserted a **15.97 mm** unchamfered peg into a **16.07 mm** unchamfered hole using a specialized compliant search; success depended on initial offset and tilt, and one **5 mm** offset case failed where **2 mm** succeeded. It is not evidence that this MiR/UR/gripper combination can routinely insert a 0.1 mm-clearance pin. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000052)

## 3. Design the printer and tools around the robot

The stated **12.5 kg arm payload and 1,300 mm reach** are useful screening inputs, but the **Robotiq 2F-85 is separately rated for 5 kg**: published specifications give **85 mm stroke**, **20–235 N programmable grip force** and about **0.9 kg gripper mass**. Include camera, changer, fingers, wiring, carried part, centre-of-gravity offset and acceleration in the *robot* payload calculation; do not interpret 235 N jaw force as a 235 N capacity for pulling a stuck door. A design study found that tool mass and a **260 mm** flange offset reduced usable payload substantially, illustrating why reach and wrist moment must be checked in each posture. For the **2.5 kg** module, nominal mass alone passes the gripper’s 5 kg rating, but an open powder container, awkward grasp, dynamic moment or hot/smooth surface can still make the grasp unsuitable. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049)

Provide a positively retained **cool-side metal handling tab or insulated carrier** for each plate; put printed parts and the plate in a tray or sealed transport cassette. A plate directly at **200 °C** requires a qualified thermal barrier, gripper-finger material and dwell-time test: neither the cited 2F-85 data nor the vacuum-gripper study establishes 200 °C operation. If using suction on *cool, clean* flat panels, provide a dedicated vacuum circuit, nonporous land, pressure confirmation and a mechanical drop catch; powder, rough surfaces and heat make suction alone a poor default. Use a changer with positively sensed tool-lock and available electrical/pneumatic pass-throughs for separate jaw, broad-plate, module-hook and cleaning tools. These are proposed design controls, not documented capabilities of the specified off-the-shelf gripper. (pqac-00000046, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000072)

For the **drop-down O-ring door**, put its operating handle outside the door’s swept arc; support its weight with a hinge counterbalance/gas strut or powered actuator, and use mechanically indexed latches or pneumatic compression rather than asking the wrist to develop seal preload. For **25–75 mm plates**, standardize the *carrier* datum and robot pickup location even if plate diameters change: use an indexed bayonet driven by a dedicated keyed tool only if its seating torque and powder tolerance are tested; a pneumatically released drawbar or zero-point chuck moves the high preload into the fixture. Design each **reservoir, recoater cartridge, cover-slide drawer, overflow jar and removable liner** with a generous grasp tab, a prescribed single extraction direction, captive detents, tapered entry/lead-ins and observable seated/unseated states. Add locating cones/kinematic features where repeatability matters, keep powder off reference lands, and support drawers and liners so extraction does not bind. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052)

Treat **100 N as documented UR10e force-mode capability, not a guaranteed UR12e force at every posture, door-opening rating, safe human-contact limit or justification to pry a jammed mechanism**. Set substantially lower task-specific search limits and verify them experimentally. A pneumatic robotic CNC vise illustrates the alternative: at **6 bar**, its lever-assisted actuator produced about **5.1 kN** clamping force with **0.35 s** clamp time, while the robot only loaded the part. A separate Haas-cell example moved **6–8 kg** castings with a **10 kg** KUKA robot and purpose-designed pneumatic three-jaw tool: these loads exceed the cited 2F-85’s **5 kg** rating. (pqac-00000058, pqac-00000060, pqac-00000076, pqac-00000077)

**Expect chips, coolant and setup to dominate reliability.** In one CNC robotic-loading implementation, chips caused imperfect part seating, washing-emulsion viscosity changed cleaning effectiveness, and slight vise-height differences upset alignment. Wrong part placement and incorrect robot recipes caused collisions and manual resets; its approximately **12-minute** unload/clean/load cycle was reported, while **140 operating hours per week was an objective, not an immediately achieved result**. For building the printer itself, two mobile arms may stage machined panels, hold a bracket while a second robot drives an accessible fastener, place standardized modules and perform prescribed functional checks. Sequence a **single arm first** on one printer fixture and one CNC fixture; use the second only where the task demonstrably needs a supporting hand or parallel servicing. A published dual-UR10e system explicitly coordinated their shared workspace with joint planning, scene updates and replanning; its application was battery disassembly, not proof of fully automatic printer assembly. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000061)

Create dimensioned CAD/URDF collision geometry for **both complete mobile manipulators**, including actual tools, camera, cable dress and each grasped plate/module as an attached object. In MoveIt’s planning scene, represent the printer enclosure, vertical-lift tray at *each commanded elevation*, door and drawer at *each commanded state*, Haas enclosure, fixture and tool rack. Check robot self-collision, robot–robot collision and all intermediate poses; check or conservatively approximate **swept volumes** of the door, drawer, trays, carried parts and arms, since checking only pickup and drop-off poses misses intervening collisions. Restrict arm movements to a verified parked-base pose and block navigation while an arm or machine aperture protrudes into a travel corridor. MoveIt/FCL has been demonstrated for two UR10e arms, with updated environmental depth data represented at **30 mm voxel** resolution; that is useful for broad obstacle avoidance but far too coarse to validate a plate edge or tight latch. A published UR/2F-85 MoveIt setup likewise explicitly models the gripper and worktable; custom dimensions and dynamic aperture states must be added for this cell. (pqac-00000061, pqac-00000062, pqac-00000063, pqac-00000079)

Test failure and recovery states—including loss of power/air, dropped plate, incomplete clamp, open powder jar and an obstructed door—before unattended runs. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000068, pqac-00000072, pqac-00000073)

The literature supplies useful analogues and component specifications, but no verified MiR250 docking guarantee, UR12e-specific maximum force-mode rating, or measured end-to-end success rate for the exact proposed configuration was established here. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000065)"}

Give concrete numbers and say clearly where you are estimating.

Two such robots could automate selected assembly steps and repetitive Haas VF-series loading, but the evidence does **not** support a claim that they could autonomously build the whole printer or execute an arbitrary prototype machining job. These are engineering judgments, not measured success rates for the proposed cell. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000065)

## 1. What LPBF automation has actually demonstrated

| Example | What worked—and what it does not establish |
|---|---|
| **HyProCell: ADIRA LPBF, EROWA robot and Haas VF-2.** Its LPBF machine gained a robot-access door, seals and automated in-chamber vacuuming. An EROWA ERD 500 transferred pallets among the printer, SOLUKON powder-removal station, magazine and Haas VF-2; a dust box contained powder during transfers. Substrate plates were **screwed to a common handling pallet**, rather than being grasped by their printed edges. The smallest CNC chamber constrained pallet size to **400 × 500 mm**. A dedicated telescopic handler accommodated loads up to **300 kg**; the reported **2 µm** is precision *after its dedicated clamp engages*, not free-space robot accuracy. A roughly **20 m** integrated layout was impractical, so scanning remained outside the physical cell. This is the closest published printer-to-Haas analogue, but uses substantial fixed industrial handling equipment, not a mobile cobot. | (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000077) |
| **Additive Industries MetalFAB1.** An Exchange Module and robot handle build plates and products; optional modules support job change, materials and post-processing. The described three-module printer has a **420 × 420 × 400 mm** build envelope. The account does not specify the gripper, latch geometry or a measured exchange success rate. | (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000017) |
| **LPBF-to-CNC zero-point interface.** Boivie and colleagues put EROWA chucks in an LPBF machine and CNC mill. Their PowerChuck P uses a **10,000 N spring clamp**, pneumatic release and **0.002 mm manufacturer-specified** pallet repeatability. Milling trials found adequate stability, but coolant migrated beneath the pallet: the interface had to be cleaned before returning to LPBF. This is precisely why the *machine fixture*, not the robot, must establish the printing and machining datums. | (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000022) |
| **Alternative part interfaces.** Ferchow and colleagues validated LPBF-integrated sacrificial bolts that act as gripping/machining datums: **250 N** produced at most **12.5 µm** displacement in one test. Their separate sheet-metal carrier reduced re-clamped deformation but measured part-position deviations up to **0.23 mm**. **Powder work is a separate automation problem.** Commercial examples combine closed powder circulation, vacuum transfer, machine-side unpacking and programmed depowdering—not an ordinary gripper carrying an open jar. contexts.context: Horstkotte et al. (2021) frames automated LPBF handling around the workpiece’s transition states throughout the process chain rather than treating printing as an isolated operation. The chain begins with L-PBF building, in which components are welded to a base plate, and continues through post-process states including excess powder, the workpiece, substrate plate, auxiliary structures, and subtractive features. These states correspond to operations such as depowdering, stress-relief annealing, substrate-plate removal, auxiliary-structure removal, and machining of subtractive features. The article describes material flow as sequences of handling functions implemented through gripping, clamping, and handling systems. Grippers provide temporary, safe contact between an object and a robot or handling device; clamping systems hold a workpiece in a defined orientation and position during processing, and carrier clamping can move workpieces through a manufacturing line without re-clamping. Handling systems transfer material between manufacturing machines or magazines and include loading and unloading. The proposed methodology generates handling-system concepts for a specified LPBF process chain and its components, beginning with analysis of handling complexity and followed by evaluation and preselection of gripping and clamping devices. contexts.context: The excerpt provides detailed safety requirements and one industrial example of automated powder handling for LPBF, but it does not describe robotic depowdering trials, MetalFAB1 modules, or interface mechanisms in detail. For powder-processing areas, it recommends sealed, easily cleanable walls; sticky mats at entrances; static-dissipative floors and walls for combustible powders; and airflow designed to capture floor-level powder and limit atmospheric exposure. Ventilation should use top-to-bottom laminar flow, floor extraction, 100% fresh air, and oxygen monitoring positioned according to gas density. Powder weighing, sieving, transport, processing, and post-processing should include emergency shutdown, smoke and heat ventilation, compliant escape routes, and Class D extinguishing agents selected using the alloy SDS. Water sprinklers and gaseous suppression are specifically discouraged in metal-powder rooms. Personnel require suitable PPE, eye showers, segregated clean/dirty PPE areas, and restricted access. The AddCreator L-PBF machine is designed for non-reactive powders such as 316L and Inconel 718 and incorporates an Automatic Closed Powder Recirculation System. Four Volkmann vacuum conveying systems transfer powder between hoppers, reducing manual handling, atmospheric exposure, and segregation. The system also supports exchangeable tables and external cleaning/part extraction, indicating an industrial automation approach, although no robotic unpacking trial results or limitations are reported here.

It recommends closed-loop powder transfer to reduce atmospheric contamination and operator contact, together with integrated temperature, humidity, and oxygen sensors for monitoring container conditions. Full digital traceability is required across powder transfers and should record splitting, blending, sieving, loading/unloading, processing, sampling, location, quantity, property data, and reuse history. For powder recovery and reuse, a reuse metric should reflect build number or cumulative exposure time, with the highest metric retained when batches are blended. Recommended starting limits are 30 builds for non-reactive powders and 10 for reactive powders, although these are not universally representative. Qualification should establish case-specific limits through exposure/build controls, test coupons, and powder-property testing. Virgin-powder refreshing is identified as a mitigation strategy, but methods must be documented and validated. Risks include oxidation, moisture ingress, contamination, powder degradation, and fire/explosion hazards from combustible powders.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides simulation-based validation of a semi-automatic vacuum unpacking system for LPBF powder removal. It evaluates nozzle length, the number and location of vacuum points, part geometry, and part height. Increasing vacuum nozzle length increases powder removal, but extending the nozzle along the full powder-bed side provides only an additional 11.24% removal compared with a 5 mm nozzle. Adding vacuum points also increases removal, with a rapid initial improvement that stabilizes after four points because the cone-shaped removal regions begin to overlap. Part geometry is a major limitation: walls can obstruct natural powder flow, and hollow cylindrical parts can trap substantial powder internally. Increasing part diameter substantially reduces recoverable powder; centred vacuum points generally perform better, although corner positioning becomes advantageous for diameters above 800 mm. Build height also affects performance: taller parts create larger vacuum cones capable of reaching powder farther from the vacuum locations, while low-height parts yield minimal removal. The excerpt therefore supports discussion of automated unpacking design trade-offs and geometric limitations, but it does not provide detailed information about powder recovery or sieving equipment, dust or explosion risks, robotic depowdering trials, MetalFAB1 modules, or industrial automation interface mechanisms.

contexts.context: This excerpt concerns Ferchow et al.’s 2022 validation of a sheet-metal clamping system for hybrid LPBF and CNC milling. The setup used a GOM ATOS Core 200 optical stereo-camera 3D scanner to compare CAD geometry, simulations, and measured sheet-metal deformation. Simulation boundary conditions included bonded LPBF-part/sheet-metal and pin/base-block interfaces, plus frictional contacts at the sheet-metal groove–pin and sheet-metal plane–base-block interfaces, both with μ = 0.2. Clamping reduced pre-existing sheet-metal flatness deformation by 44% on average. After LPBF, releasing the clamps increased deformation by 500%; reclamping for milling reduced it by 61%. The average maximum part-position deviations after LPBF were 0.034 mm in x and 0.165 mm in y, with an overall maximum deviation of 0.23 mm before milling and the same absolute maximum reported during milling. Dynamic stability was evaluated using an impact hammer, piezoelectric accelerometer, signal acquisition, and frequency-response analysis; the excerpt reports natural-frequency peaks for several LPBF geometries. Milling used a MAHO machine and cooling lubricant, with various end, ball, and roughing mills. contexts.context: Boivie et al. (2011) describe an Erowa PowerChuck P zero-point clamping system used in the hybrid LPBF/CNC cell. The movable pallet is held to the chuck by spring-generated clamping force of 10,000 N, released using compressed air. The manufacturer-specified pallet-to-PowerChuck positioning repeatability is 0.002 mm. The apparatus comprised the Erowa chuck and pallet, with milling stability evaluated in a Bridgeport VMC whose stiffness and spindle characteristics were considered comparable to the intended DM machine. Tests used mild steel of approximately 260 HB hardness and a Ø20 mm indexable-carbide end mill, with both side-milling and slot-milling conditions. The tests examined machining near the clamping center and at unsupported workpiece ends; no apparent difference in stability or vibration was found, and no large vibrations occurred. The authors concluded that the Erowa system was probably sufficiently strong and stable for the planned milling tasks. The main observed issue was not clamp failure but cutting-fluid penetration into the pallet and chuck, leaving fluid beneath the pallet; thorough cleaning was therefore required before transferring the setup to the additive machine. contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial information on Ferchow et al.’s 2021 hybrid LPBF–CNC clamping demonstrations, but it does not report EROWA zero-point measurements, exact locator precision, robotic-gripper forces, or the Ferchow 2022 experiments. In the robotic-housing case, three integrated vertical bolts were placed on non-functional surfaces; two had 4 mm diameters and one had a 3.7 mm diameter. The bolts used a predefined stepwise notch and enabled five-sided machining without re-clamping. A hybrid metallic sheet was fixed to the machine base plate with nine countersunk screws and removed after processing by releasing those screws, avoiding sawing or erosion. Nineteen surfaces were machined with three tools. The bolts were printed on a curved surface of 10 mm radius. No chatter was observed, and the maximum measured roughness was Ra = 0.9 µm. After machining, bolts could be sheared off with a wrench without residual material. LPBF-related thermal and local deformations occurred; the maximum deviation attributed to the bolts at the clamped position was 0.3 mm. For the aircraft-bracket case, conventional clamping was considered potentially damaging to the fragile topology-optimized structure. The proposed design separated the shaft and clamping ball, using a reusable LPBF cap with wings and a snap-fit connection; this was intended to support automated robotic handling while avoiding manually removed support structures.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Boivie et al.’s positioning-accuracy investigation for the ConceptLaser M2 hybrid manufacturing cell, but it does not identify an EROWA zero-point system or report an exact numerical EROWA precision. The apparatus consisted of a solid metal block fastened to the build plate and a digital indicator gauge with micron accuracy positioned in the process station. Repeated carrier movements were tested: the carrier was moved fully to the manual powder-handling station and returned to the process station, with 33 measurements taken in each axis. A second, smaller test moved only the base plate 140 mm up and down and measured X and Y deviations. The Z-axis zero position was reconfigured in the handling station before each measurement. The full carrier-motion tests showed deviations that, on most occasions, exceeded the gauge accuracy; the smaller base-plate movements produced lower deviations. The authors interpreted the results as indicating that carrier positioning had an insignificant effect on overall machine accuracy. contexts.context: The excerpt provides partial information about Ferchow et al.’s 2022 sheet-metal clamping-system study, but it does not report the exact zero-point EROWA measured precision, nor does it identify Boivie 2011 papers. It describes a disposable sheet-metal profile used as an interface between an LPBF part, handling, and clamping system, with the sheet metal intended to facilitate access to both sides during milling. A finite-element simulation and a 3×3×3 full-factorial experiment investigated sheet-metal thickness, clamping distance, and part length. Sheet-metal thickness was the statistically significant main factor; clamping distance and part length had minor, statistically insignificant effects. The tested thicknesses were 1, 3, and 5 mm, while clamping distances were 45, 52.5, and 60 mm. Measured flatness ranged from 0.008 to 1.766 mm across the listed trials. The authors concluded that increasing thickness substantially reduced deformation and proposed 2 mm as a compromise for the clamping-system design. The excerpt contains no apparatus specification beyond LPBF simulation and milling context, no plate-locator or robotic-gripper description, no clamping-force measurements, and no failure-mode analysis.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides accuracy figures for the SIMO platform built on a MiR250 mobile base, but it does not report a dedicated measured docking repeatability or absolute-accuracy experiment using VL markers, nor does it mention a UR10e mobile manipulator. The MiR250’s odometry-based pose estimate is reported as ±50 mm, while computer vision and SLAM for a typical mobile base are described as achieving approximately ±10 mm—insufficient for microplate handling. The docking/positioning procedure therefore combines SLAM navigation to a waypoint, VL-marker localization, wrist-camera vision, and six-point tactile/contact registration. Robot1 estimates the instrument pose visually, then refines it by touching three perpendicular faces; Robot2 uses the refined pose to place the plate at the instrument handover position. The excerpt states that the method can compensate for rare outliers through real-time visual and tactile corrections and can tolerate small unexpected instrument movements. A ±1.2 mm precision value appears in the passage, but the supplied text does not clearly identify whether this is repeatability, absolute docking accuracy, or specifically the result after vision alone versus contact registration. Thus, the excerpt supports a distinction between coarse mobile-base/navigation accuracy (±50 mm odometry or ±10 mm SLAM/vision) and finer instrument-relative positioning using visual plus tactile registration, but it does not explicitly establish that ±1 mm was achieved.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns experimental force-mode behavior of a UR5e collaborative robot, not the UR10e, Robotiq 2F-85, or finishing experiments specifically requested. It describes tests in the 1–10 N low-force range, using an OptoForce Hex six-axis force/torque sensor mounted at the wrist to compare commanded/set values with physically measured forces. The results show that a 10 N setpoint produced actual mean forces from 8.95 N to 13.26 N depending on workspace position. Across setpoints from 1 N to 10 N, the average deviation was approximately 0.38 N, with a maximum deviation of 0.61 N at workspace limits. The study also varied task position, force level, and force-mode controller parameters. Recommended settings were Gain 0.5/Damping 0.7 for 1–4 N, Gain 1.0/Damping 0.6 for 5–7 N, and Gain 2.0/Damping 0.8 for 8–10 N. These data may help distinguish a force-mode commanded setpoint from the resulting measured contact force, but the excerpt provides no UR10e-specific quantitative setpoints, safety contact-force ceiling, joint-stall comparison, Robotiq 2F-85 maximum force or payload, or UR10e finishing results.

contexts.context: This excerpt concerns the UR5e, not the UR10e, and it does not provide the requested quantitative UR10e setpoints, UR10e finishing experiments, joint-stall-versus-force-mode comparison, or Robotiq 2F-85 maximum force and payload specifications. It does, however, offer context relevant to interpreting low-force control limits. The UR5e documentation cited in the paper gives a force/torque sensor accuracy figure of 4 N, while prior work reportedly indicates that contact forces below 2 N are generally not controlled using force mode effectively. The authors identify external disturbances, joint friction, kinematic configuration, inertial forces, and limited manipulability as important causes of poor low-force reproduction. Force-control performance degrades particularly near workspace boundaries and singular configurations. The paper also reports that, for a 10 N target in one experiment, dynamic overshoot averaged approximately 146.42%, potentially damaging a workpiece in precision machining. These findings should not be treated as a safety contact-force ceiling: the excerpt discusses sensor accuracy, commanded-force tracking, overshoot, and practical control capability, which are distinct from a formally specified protective-contact limit. No evidence here establishes UR10e-specific force-mode command ranges or a safety-rated maximum contact force.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports experimental force-mode behavior for a UR5e, not a UR10e, and therefore does not establish UR10e setpoints, force limits, joint-stall behavior, or finishing performance. The tested commanded interaction-force range was 1–10 N. Force fidelity was strongly nonlinear: low setpoints were difficult to achieve and produced higher RMSE and MAE, while performance improved at higher forces; beyond approximately 6 N, the Rate fz measure approached 100%. Gain and damping were important, especially from 1–4 N, where gain above 0.5 could cause overshoot changes exceeding 200–300% and oscillation; low gain with high damping was recommended. For 5–7 N, gain around 0.5 provided a favorable dynamics/precision tradeoff, while 8–10 N generally showed smaller RMSE and P10/P20 values up to about 95%. Overall stable gain/damping regions were reported, but these are UR5e controller-tuning results rather than universal force ceilings. The excerpt also states that accuracy degrades near singular configurations and that force mode may be locked for some configurations. It contains no data on Robotiq 2F-85 maximum force or payload, no UR10e finishing experiments, and no explicit safety contact-force ceiling. Thus, commanded force-mode setpoints must be distinguished from externally imposed safety contact limits; this passage addresses the former only.

For surface finishing, the TCP z-axis must be configured as the compliant axis, and the force-control task frame must track the current TCP frame during motion. contexts.context: Xydas et al. (39th Annual Small Satellite Conference) describe a MiR250 carrying a mobile lighting trolley, controlled through a custom ROS2 API wrapper. The facility used 34 Vicon cameras and periodic calibration (typically under 15 minutes). Although KUKAs repeat end-effector poses within 1 mm relative to their bases, environmental and frame-alignment errors produced about 10 mm uncertainty per metre before correction. After calibration, standalone flange accuracy was 2–3 mm; Vicon benchmarking achieved 3.2 mm average and 7.2 mm maximum relative error, theoretically reducible to 0.5 mm with improved camera mounting, resolution, and marker targets.
contexts.question:
We are checking whether a UR12e collaborative arm (the renamed UR10e: 12.5 kg payload, 1300 mm reach) with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper and a wrist camera, riding on a MiR250 mobile base, can tend a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion machine that sits on a vertical lift module tray: open and close a drop-down chamber door sealed by an O-ring, exchange a 25 to 75 mm heated (200 C) build plate held by a bayonet or a drawbar, swap powder reservoirs and recoater blade cartridges, pull a cover-slide drawer, empty an overflow jar, lift out chamber liners for cleaning, and exchange a 2.5 kg build module that leaves through the chamber floor. We also want to know whether two such mobile arms could do the machine's assembly and the machine tending of a Haas VF-series CNC mill to make its parts.

Please summarise, with sources: (1) published and industrial examples of robotic or automated LPBF tending (build plate and build module exchange, depowdering, unpacking, sieving, zero-point clamping and plate interfaces, door and hatch actuation, cobots vs industrial robots, mobile manipulators) and what made them work or fail; (2) mobile manipulator accuracy: MiR docking repeatability, the need for fiducial or camera re-registration, and achievable placement accuracy for peg-in-hole and zero-point engagement; (3) end-of-arm tooling for this kind of work: tool changers, custom fingertips, vacuum cups, compliance units, and how to design machine features (handles, lead-ins, chamfers, kinematic couplings, detents) so a cobot can work them; (4) force limits: how much force a UR10e/UR12e can apply in force mode and how designs avoid needing more (pneumatic clamps, toggle latches pulled by actuators, gas struts); (5) robotic CNC machine tending with cobots: loading vises and pneumatic fixtures, payload limits, chip and coolant problems, door opening, and what fraction of a prototype job's operations are realistic; (6) collision checking and motion planning practice for these cells (MoveIt, FCL, swept volumes, safety zones). Give concrete numbers and say clearly where you are estimating.

contexts.context: Gadringer et al., *Mechanical Sciences* 13 (2022), pp. 361–370, DOI:10.5194/ms-13-361-2022, compare UR10e force control with active compliance. UR10e is six-axis, 10-kg payload, 500-Hz control (2-ms cycle), nominal force control up to 100 N with 5.5-N accuracy. Impedance control uses desired pose/trajectory, joint states, and six-axis contact wrench, but requires an accurate robot dynamic model and task-specific settings. An active pneumatic compliance device (ACF) instead decouples robot motion from contact forces, allowing position control; pressure is regulated using sensors, sometimes load cells or orientation calibration. Tests used an ATI Delta SI-660-60 sensor (1,980-N range; 0.25-N normal-force resolution; 800-µs sampling).

contexts.context: This excerpt provides Bian et al. (2023) methodology and hardware context, but it does not include the numerical docking-positioning results or fiducial-reader measurement table needed to quantify absolute accuracy and repeatability. The FiMa-Reader uses an infrared camera with nearby 940 nm fill-lights, a Linux-based embedded processor containing two Cortex-A72 and four Cortex-A53 cores, and Ethernet output. The experiments were designed to compare repeatable docking positioning accuracy from FiMa-Reader against a LiDAR-based navigation process, assess different output rates associated with the multithread framework, and evaluate operation with lights on and off. For marker-performance testing, the study compared the DAH pattern with ArUco, Data Matrix, and Data Matrix with Box markers. The markers were printed at 50 mm size on the same surface material, and images were collected across clean, cage-textured, line-textured, and indoor backgrounds, with random occlusion examples. The infrared illumination constrained the camera-to-marker test range to approximately 50–250 mm. The excerpt also states that pose estimation uses the previous valid frame pose or IPPE result as an initial value and refines it by minimizing reprojection error over four marker corners. No results from Scamarcio (2025), Karimov (2024), or NIST Aboul-Enein (2023) are present here.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides a quantitative absolute positioning result for Scamarcio et al. (2025): after vision-based instrument localization and six-point touch feedback, R2 transfers a plate to the instrument handover frame with a reported precision of ±1.2 mm. The passage distinguishes three strategies relevant to separating docking, visual positioning, and touch refinement. VL uses a visual marker for fine positioning, with the handover pose hardcoded for the benchmark; CV estimates the handover pose from computer vision without pose refinement; and CV + TF refines the instrument pose using touch feedback before estimating the handover position. All methods use SLAM for navigation, so the excerpt does not provide a standalone numerical accuracy for MiR/SLAM docking. The instrument marker is an STag attached at different locations depending on the instrument, while VL is a separate fine-positioning marker. The listed instruments include a mockup, plate reader, plate sealer, and pipetting station, with touch-point constraints varying by geometry. The reported ANOVA and Tukey results establish statistically significant differences in success rates among CV, CV + TF, and VL, but no actual success-rate values or standard-deviation numbers are visible in this excerpt. It therefore supports the Scamarcio touch-refined handover precision, but not a complete absolute-versus-repeatability comparison or the requested fiducial-reader table values from the other sources.

contexts.context: Bian et al. (2023) reports fiducial-reader detection and docking-positioning results that can support a comparison with other docking studies, although this excerpt does not contain the Scamarcio (2025), Karimov (2024), or NIST Aboul-Enein (2023) results. For marker reading, the reported table gives data capacity, detection rate, and average detection time for original and randomly occluded image datasets. The DAH pattern achieved 97% detection and 11.06 ms average detection time on original images; under occlusion it achieved 67.3% and 23.56 ms. ArUco achieved 70% and 24.58 ms originally, falling to 4.5% and 27.61 ms under occlusion. Data Matrix achieved 19% and 14.01 ms originally, and 0.2% and 44.56 ms under occlusion. Data Matrix with Box achieved 84% and 12.05 ms originally, and 7.2% and 20.28 ms under occlusion. In the AMR experiment, a PGV100 sensor with 0.1 mm and 0.1° measurement resolution recorded relative pose to a ground-mounted marker. Across 1500 repetitions, docking versus pure navigation produced x ranges of 8.4 versus 61.9 mm, y ranges of 4.7 versus 8.5 mm, and angular ranges of 0.30° versus 1.9°, corresponding to reported improvements of 86.42%, 44.7%, and 84.21%, respectively. These are repeatability/distribution-range results rather than an absolute ground-truth bias measurement.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not identify the NIST Aboul-Enein 2023 report or NIST 2258, nor does it describe point-cloud fiducials or a specific peg-placement experiment. It does provide closely related mobile-manipulator calibration and endpoint-positioning results. A mobile AGV navigation sensor supplies the vehicle pose, while manipulator measurements are transformed into a stationary world frame using the calibration transform between the AGV and manipulator. The calibration was evaluated using manual and Ceres Solver methods: manual calibration produced a base offset of (831.5, -7.5) mm, 90.6° rotation, 1.25 mm mean-square error, and 6.3 mm maximum residual; Ceres produced (833.6, -8.2) mm, 90.53° rotation, and 1.19 mm mean-square error. The computed offset allowed the end effector to reach within a few millimeters of the target despite varying AGV position and orientation, reducing subsequent search time. The excerpt attributes residual positioning limits to random and systematic AGV navigation-sensor errors. It also presents a two-dimensional robot-world/hand-eye calibration formulation and reports maximum successive-target distance uncertainties of 0.09 mm for an iterative solution and 0.04 mm for a closed-form solution.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a multifunctional aerospace drilling end-effector (ACME) mounted on a UR collaborative robot. It describes a compliant end-effector coupling (CEEC) for vertical peg-in-hole assembly. The stated challenge is that SCARA robots may repeat taught points within 0.025 mm yet fail parts having only 0.020 mm clearance. The authors identify chamfers or lead-ins as necessary for conventional passive correction, while their design uses an air bearing intended to provide zero lateral stiffness and accommodate lateral and rotational misalignment. Their “free” assembly strategy allows the peg to slide sideways during downward motion; a separate “lock” strategy makes the wrist stiff for rapid parts transportation. The coupling also isolates assembly forces and allows insertion-force adjustment through a variable air spring. An RT2000 Seiko robot is cited as capable of up to 16 kg downward assembly force, with the compliant wrist acting as a shock absorber to reduce force transmitted to parts. These data may inform gripper compliance and insertion design, but no metal/powder handling results, vacuum performance, high-temperature operation, or commercial gripper/tool-changer specifications are reported.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a vision-driven compliant insertion system, but it does not report the specific experimental values in the question: an initial tolerance of ±2.5 mm and ±3°, a maximum insertion force below 5.34 N, 0.1 mm clearance relative to metrology, or UR mobile-base re-registration accuracy of 1.2 mm. Instead, it reports a Barrett WAM arm with translational errors as large as 2.6 cm and uses visual servoing, hand compliance, and coordinated spiral insertion to accommodate positioning errors and reduce jamming. The insertion process maintains a small downward force against the hole edges while aligning the object, and experiments achieved success rates from 8/12 to 11/12 depending on object shape. contexts.context: The excerpt concerns calibration and positioning accuracy for a mobile manipulator, rather than an experimental peg-in-hole tolerance or insertion-force study. It describes estimating the manipulator mounting offset from paired AGV and robot measurements using a 2D transformation model and Ceres Solver. contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that the CNC-tending system operates with strict spatial requirements and that the gripper has a narrow tolerance envelope: empirical project data indicate that TCP deviations exceeding ±2.0 mm prevent proper finger engagement. The deterministic ID-to-Recipe architecture executes pre-recorded joint-space motions without real-time visual servoing or force-torque feedback, so mechanical displacement, slipping, and tolerance changes remain uncorrected. These errors can accumulate across repeated cycles and ultimately cause part misplacement or failure to engage CNC fixtures. The excerpt does not report the specific experimental peg-in-hole limits of ±2.5 mm and ±3°, the maximum insertion force of less than 5.34 N, the 0.1 mm clearance comparison against metrology, or the 1.2 mm UR mobile-base re-registration result and associated success. It therefore cannot distinguish experimentally between passive chamfer capture and the resultant system-level tolerance. It only provides a related gripper-engagement tolerance and explains why open-loop execution is vulnerable to drift. The cited ±2.0 mm limit should not be treated as equivalent to peg-in-hole capture tolerance, insertion-force performance, clearance, or mobile-base registration accuracy.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited engineering evidence relevant to CNC robotic machine tending. It reports a published collaborative work-cell testbed in which UR3 robots and CNC machine emulators were coordinated by a centralized PLC supervisor. The system used Modbus for robot communication and TwinCAT ADS for machine tools, demonstrating real-time, safety-aware robot–machine interaction. More broadly, the review states that PLCs are well suited to deterministic sequencing and low-level synchronization, but that PLC-only integration is rigid, difficult to scale, and limited in data richness. Higher-level protocols or middleware may therefore be needed for monitoring, diagnostics, and digital-twin connectivity. However, the excerpt does not document a Haas VF cell, actual vise loading, pneumatic clamping, automatic doors, coolant or chip interference, the number of automated operations, or setup limitations. contexts.context: The excerpt documents MoveIt/FCL-based collision monitoring for a dual-UR10e system operating in a shared workspace. FCL runs within the MoveIt Planning Scene, which monitors both robot models and environmental collision objects in real time. Inter-robot checking uses a digital-twin arrangement: each robot’s URDF embeds a replica of the other robot, while MoveIt’s Allowed Collision Matrix encodes feasible body interactions and excludes irrelevant body pairs to reduce computational cost. Environmental perception comes from an Intel RealSense depth camera; MoveIt’s Occupancy Map Updater converts depth data into a 0.03 m voxel-resolution OctoMap, which is published to both robots’ planning scenes. The reactive loop updates the planning scene from sensors and robot-state feedback, queries collision state and minimum distance, stops execution upon collision, and invokes avoidance plus replanning when distance falls below threshold ε. Detected contact points are visualized in RViz. The excerpt also mentions dynamic obstacles generally, but it does not specifically document attached parts, grippers, held objects, swept-volume checking, doors, drawers, trays, safety-rated zones, non-safety-rated planning, machining cells, or LPBF cells. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general collision-checking guidance relevant to documenting a robot machining or LPBF cell. A robot is modeled as articulated rigid links that must avoid collisions with static or movable obstacles, the environment, and other robot links. This is especially important for coordinated dual-arm operation in overlapping workspaces. contexts.context: Bonifazio documents practical CNC robot-tending trials involving automated loading and unloading, rather than chip or coolant clearing, automatic-door operation, or vise actuation. The main failures were incorrect operator placement of raw parts in jigs, rotated or misaligned parts, gripper-to-jig collisions, positioning errors, and pick-up/drop-off points that could not consistently meet the required tolerance. These failures caused repeated cycle interruptions, manual resets, rejected parts, and loss of production during unattended night shifts. The CNC’s Renishaw probe rejected parts that were positioned excessively out of tolerance, while parameter adjustments for both the part and robot increased downtime. Mitigations included operator training, visual setup instructions, standardized error-handling procedures, redesigned dedicated jigs, fixed pitch distances between parts, and robot “recipes” containing raw/finished dimensions and jig positioning information. contexts.context: Bonifazio describes practical CNC machine-tending operations for an automated robotic cell handling semi-finished, finished, and raw hydraulic-block parts. The cycle consists of unloading, pallet cleaning, and reloading. During unloading, a tipper rotates parts so unfinished surfaces are exposed for gripping; finished pieces are placed on a separate inclined-plane location. After unloading, bay shutters close automatically and a high-pressure emulsion jet washes chips and debris from the pallet. Reported failures included residual chips that interfered with semi-finished-part positioning, emulsion-viscosity fluctuations that caused incomplete cleaning, and small vise-height variations that compromised alignment. Improvements included revising the washing cycle, adding piece-presence checks with gripper proximity sensors, and training staff to reduce recipe-related collision stops. The robot could skip empty or incorrectly loaded drawer positions, preventing disrupted loading cycles. The reported average cycle time was approximately 12 minutes, with a longer-term objective of 140 operating hours per CNC machine per week. This excerpt provides concrete machine-tending procedures and failure lessons relevant to high-mix production, but it does not report prototype-specific trials, robot payload limits, or detailed payload-related constraints. It also refers to automatically closing bay shutters rather than explicitly documenting CNC door actuation.

contexts.context: This excerpt is a relevant source for general robot and collaborative-platform safety risk assessment, but it does not fully document every safety topic in the question. The authors report a holistic assessment covering the cobot, humans, environment, and auxiliary equipment, with 55 hazardous situations evaluated across six categories under risk indexes and the draft ISO 10218-2. Relevant hazards include thermal exposure from sparks and hot surfaces, combustible-process dust, pneumatic hazards, rotating-disc contact, compliance-head ejection, and workpiece ejection. Controls include mandatory protective clothing and eye/face protection, a dust-collection system designed according to NFPA-484, emergency pneumatic shutoff, secured hoses, AIRSKIN, emergency-stop buttons, a tool-changer locking system, safety shoes, and clamping. Two laser scanners detect operator proximity and stop disc rotation; however, the authors state that this solution still requires industrial validation. The excerpt does not mention ISO/TS 15066, pinch-point hazards specifically, safety-rated monitored stop terminology, a 200°C hot plate, laser powder, CNC spindle/tool hazards, an independent PLC interlock, or an explicit statement that collaborative robots are not automatically safe. It therefore supports general safeguarding and risk-assessment claims rather than those specific technical assertions.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a robotic CNC cell using an NGV MM 150 vise on a zero-point/perforated base. A 50×50-mm pneumatic cylinder with a 2.6:1 lever produced measured clamping forces of 3.4–5.8 kN at 4–7 bar; at 6 bar, approximately 5.1 kN, with 0.35-s clamp and 0.30-s release times. Zero-point resets reportedly achieved ±0.01 mm repeatability. Sensors, 5/3 valves, pressure monitoring, PLC interlocks, and CNC-door coordination supported safe automation. Testing covered 100,000 cycles, including chip/emulsion exposure, without play beyond tolerance. (AGIR Bulletin 4/2025, pp. 14–15.)
contexts.question:
We are checking whether a UR12e collaborative arm (the renamed UR10e: 12.5 kg payload, 1300 mm reach) with a Robotiq 2F-85 gripper and a wrist camera, riding on a MiR250 mobile base, can tend a small lab-built laser powder bed fusion machine that sits on a vertical lift module tray: open and close a drop-down chamber door sealed by an O-ring, exchange a 25 to 75 mm heated (200 C) build plate held by a bayonet or a drawbar, swap powder reservoirs and recoater blade cartridges, pull a cover-slide drawer, empty an overflow jar, lift out chamber liners for cleaning, and exchange a 2.5 kg build module that leaves through the chamber floor. We also want to know whether two such mobile arms could do the machine's assembly and the machine tending of a Haas VF-series CNC mill to make its parts.

Please summarise, with sources: (1) published and industrial examples of robotic or automated LPBF tending (build plate and build module exchange, depowdering, unpacking, sieving, zero-point clamping and plate interfaces, door and hatch actuation, cobots vs industrial robots, mobile manipulators) and what made them work or fail; (2) mobile manipulator accuracy: MiR docking repeatability, the need for fiducial or camera re-registration, and achievable placement accuracy for peg-in-hole and zero-point engagement; (3) end-of-arm tooling for this kind of work: tool changers, custom fingertips, vacuum cups, compliance units, and how to design machine features (handles, lead-ins, chamfers, kinematic couplings, detents) so a cobot can work them; (4) force limits: how much force a UR10e/UR12e can apply in force mode and how designs avoid needing more (pneumatic clamps, toggle latches pulled by actuators, gas struts); (5) robotic CNC machine tending with cobots: loading vises and pneumatic fixtures, payload limits, chip and coolant problems, door opening, and what fraction of a prototype job's operations are realistic; (6) collision checking and motion planning practice for these cells (MoveIt, FCL, swept volumes, safety zones). Give concrete numbers and say clearly where you are estimating.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an industrial CNC-tending cell (internship dissertation, pp. 11–15): a robot unloads/loads pallets, uses a tipper and inclined plane for gripping, and relies on Modula-drawer templates and recipe data instead of vision. Average cycle time is approximately 12 minutes, targeting 140 machine-hours/week. Problems included vise-height variation, residual chips, emulsion-viscosity-dependent cleaning, missing/misplaced parts, and recipe-related collision errors. Improvements included proximity-sensor presence checks, better washing, staff training, robot collision detection, and an emergency stop. Siemens PLC coordination supported repeatability; templates and verification were key enablers.
